title: Our search for beauty is what makes us human
subtitle: We are pattern seeking creatures
author: Nicholas Humphrey
introduction: As humans, we are fascinated by beauty in the world. With so much of it around us, it is natural to wonder whether it is a luxury or a necessary part of how we interact with the world. In this interview with the IAI's Ozbir Kip, neuropsychologist Nicholas Humphrey argues that the essence of beauty is rhyme and that we are programmed to seek connections and patterns across nature, art and music.
body:
To discover more about the nature of beauty, come to the HowTheLightGetsIn festival on September 19-20th to hear Heather Widdows, Babette Babich, and Dasha Nekrasova on the theme "Too Beautiful To Be True." Buy tickets now.

Kip: You have a very broad area of research spanning the fields of psychology, evolutionary biology, neuroscience, and philosophy. What is it that makes you think these fields should be studied together?

Humphrey: I have always thought of psychology as being the central topic, or question, of our minds and how they give us a picture of the world we live in. I became a psychologist to begin with, but gradually, I drifted towards philosophy, partly because I always found myself asking questions which went beyond what I could immediately begin to study experimentally, especially when I went out to do field work in Africa with gorillas, and I came back with some big questions which I thought were going to be better addressed at a theoretical, philosophical level, and I haven’t looked back.

And are there things that philosophers can learn from the field of neuropsychology, in your opinion?

Yes, of course. I think philosophers can get a lot of correctives from science and from psychology. In a way, new ideas about the philosophy of mind have been driven increasingly by results from brain damage, from psychopathology, from evolutionary theory.

The phenomenon of blindsight, for example, which I think is one of the most crucial findings in the study of consciousness, shows that you can separate cognition from phenomenal experience. This is the phenomenon that occurs after damage to the visual cortex, where you can show that a subject can see—initially it was a monkey, but now, of course, we’ve studied human beings. They can tell the shape, color and dimensions of objects, where they are, their relationship to each other, and yet they’ll say all the time, “Yes, doctor, but there’s nothing there; I’m not having any experience.”

Ideas can rhyme, concepts can rhyme—it’s not only sensory phenomena.

That’s a very surprising finding. I think philosophers have still not taken on board quite what it means. It drives a wedge between what I’ve called cognitive consciousness and phenomenal consciousness. Cognitive consciousness is to do with computing perceptions, memory, decision-making, and so on. I think that it uses a global workspace, and it was a clever invention in the course of the history of our animal minds, and I think it goes back a very long way, deep into the animal kingdom. Lots of animals have cognitive consciousness: frogs and snakes, and probably bumblebees as well. Very few animals have phenomenal consciousness. It may be restricted, I believe, to animals which have evolved in the last 200 million years, chiefly, and perhaps exclusively, mammals and birds.

In your latest book, you talk about how humans have adapted to seek, enjoy, and cherish beauty in the world. How do you characterize beauty?

I started off with a behavioral definition—not beauty, but visual preferences. What do animals choose to look at, and equally, what do humans choose to look at? The time I was doing that early research, I was thinking beyond the findings I was getting in the lab. I don’t have a background in aesthetics, but in reading widely, I came across an essay by the wonderful poet Gerard Manley Hopkins.

This was an essay he’d written for his tutor at Oxford, in which he discusses the origins of beauty, and it struck me as the best and most to-the-point discussion of beauty that actually exists in either science or philosophy. What Hopkins does [in the essay] is take his professor for a walk in the garden of his college in Oxford, and he takes examples from around him. Particularly, he starts off with the fan of the chestnut tree—seven leaves linked together to form that beautiful fan.

It looks perfect to us, but why? What is it that appeals to us about it? He analyzes it in terms of what he calls visual rhyme. He shows how the leaves are examples of “alike, but different.” Essentially, they’re the same shape, but they’re different in detail, and he builds on that to say, look at the rest of the garden; listen to the bird song, consider better, grander examples of poetry. And again and again, come back to the finding that what’s driving our delight in these phenomena is rhyme, the comparisons we make between things, and the ways in which they resemble but differ from each other. In other words, things belonging to the same class but being different examples of it.

SUGGESTED READING Philosophy must embrace poetry By John Gibson

In my book, I try and produce some semi-formal definitions of rhyme in order to talk about different kinds of phenomena, because I want to use the term “rhyme” even more broadly than Hopkins does. I think that ideas can rhyme, concepts can rhyme—it’s not only sensory phenomena. We can get rhyme in mathematics; we can get rhyme in metaphor and so on. In fact, take the example of metaphor, where we draw an analogy between two things which share some essential feature, but nonetheless are different examples of it. It’s a clear case of what Hopkins would have called rhyme. It’s a very broad definition, but it actually engages with an awful lot of what we call beauty.

Sometimes we like things because they’re not beautiful, because they actually break the rules, and that becomes interesting in its own right. We must also remember that things we find beautiful also, to some extent, define us, and so again and again in the history of art, we found that people adopt new standards of beauty in order to say: “Look at me! This is where I stand in relation to the history of my subject and my art.”

How would you characterize the difference between art and craft? Both can display rhyme in different ways; the rhyme that exists in a well-made watch is arguably different from the rhyme that we see in Van Gogh’s Starry Night, for example. Would it make sense to say that they are beautiful in the same way, or are there different kinds of beauty in the world?

I think they’re beautiful in some of the same ways, but of course one is much more elaborate, much more complex, much more interesting than the other. Art often requires some kind of education to see what’s going on in it, to realize the way in which an artist has exploited rhyme in the arrangements on the canvas or in the music he or she has created. So we have to learn to see rhyme. We have to get better at analyzing it, and I think one of the glories of growing up is that we actually find more and more beauty in the world the more we know, the more we understand. The next generation of human beings will find rhymes and beauty and make forms of art which we haven’t even imagined yet.

To come back to the difference between craft and these other forms of beauty, there’s one thing which I’ve begun increasingly to think is particularly important, which is the way in which we pay attention to the role of the artist. If someone makes a fine pot, or designs a perfect sword, we know that there is a craftsman there. They are artists, but we don’t think of them as being emotionally involved in what they were doing. Whereas artists go beyond craft and have actually put themselves and their emotions center stage. They’ve picked out things in the world to respond to, and it’s often argued that our appreciation of high art depends on us somehow channeling the emotion of the artist at the time he or she made that work of art.

One thing which convinces me again and again about the importance of the artist is the plain fact, which has been commented on by everybody from Clive Bell onwards, that we don’t like fakes. We care about whether work has been produced as a copy by somebody who wasn’t involved in its creation, even if it has all the same balance and harmony in it. It doesn’t contain what Bell called significant form. Bell defined significant form as when we were experiencing the same motion that the artist did in making the work of art. Where there is an artist, we feel differently about a work of art, and it’s why there’s been so much debate recently about, for example, music or painting produced by machines. Machines can produce things which are as formally beautiful as a Bach prelude or sonata, and they’re beginning to make paintings, which can be mistaken for Cézannes or Picassos.

One of the psychological effects, and it can be measured, is that people feel small in the presence of awesome beauty.

When people are asked whether they find them beautiful, and they’re told they’re looking at a work of art by a human artist, they find it much more impressive than when the very same work of art is presented to them as the work of a machine. If it actually is the work of a machine, and they’re told it’s the work of a human artist, they value it more highly than if they had believed it was by a machine.

I think this tells us something very significant about how we humans respond to the natural world. We find the world beautiful in the ways we do because again and again we really don’t believe that there wasn’t an artist involved. We look at a landscape or a sunset or a flower meadow, and we can’t but see the hand of a designer behind it. It’s been said that human beings are natural-born creationists. It’s second nature to us to imagine a designer, an intelligent and supremely gifted designer.

In the case of natural beauty, to whom do we attribute this beauty—a creator? How is this different to the argument for God’s existence from design?

The argument from design was very strong before Darwin came along and showed us another way of doing it. There was really no alternative but to imagine that some supernatural being must have been responsible, and Paley’s famous argument about the watchmaker was held as a very rational argument. Only when we have found an alternative could we say we don’t need God.

SUGGESTED VIEWING The god desire With David Baddiel

Without the belief in God or in at least a creator, we wouldn’t have the same feelings about the beauties of nature, and it’s why I think—and I think that it’s a rather important point to make—human beings have an appreciation for beauty, which just isn’t present in any non-human animals. Dogs simply don’t admire sunsets; chimpanzees don’t go out there and listen to the sounds of the birds. They show some interest, maybe, in natural phenomena, but I don’t think it affects them in the same way, because it doesn’t occur to them to think that they were made by another intelligent being.

Does the personal benefit gained from believing in a creator outweigh the potential harms it may have on society?

I think they’re incommensurate in a way. They occur in different spheres of life. I think religion is the most dangerous force in the world today at a political level, because of the divisions and the sense of superiority it creates, especially amongst religions, which believe that only the members of that religion—as the chosen ones—actually deserve to live in the world created by their God. And I think we all hoped that the world would become more and more rational over this past hundred years. It’s actually been going backwards in ways which we could hardly have imagined.

Despite being beneficial, beauty can be enjoyed irresponsibly. History is full of people whose obsession with beauty led them to their demise. The story of Antoni Gaudí comes to mind, who, when taking steps back to see the grandeur of La Sagrada Familia, got hit by a bus, which led to his death. We can say that beauty can also mislead, in the form of senseless rhyme, as you mention in the book. Is there a danger to appreciating rhyme and beauty, and how is this danger best managed?

Scholarship is dangerous too; look at how many people have died in the course of trying to get to a deeper understanding of the world. Look at Archimedes, who was murdered by soldiers on the beach because he was too busy drawing circles and working out theorems in the sand. Enthusiasms can create accidents in many different spheres of life. In the particular case of our attraction to rhyme and beauty, I do agree.

Human consciousness is an astonishing creation, which has depended on a whole chapter of accidents in the evolution of human beings.

I discuss, in the book, what I regard as the kind of perversion of our attraction to rhyme, and that’s the way in which it can lead to obsessive hobbies, collecting mad things simply because they all fit so beautifully into categories and that we can enjoy staring. We enjoy stamp collecting and bird egg collecting, and can sit for hours just admiring the rhyme and variation, which exists within this very small subset of the world.

Bird spotting or stamp collecting isn’t so different from listening to music, which we find lovely only because of the rhymes and assonances that exist within the work, in exactly the way that a stamp collector would say they would in his collection of stamps, or the bird collector would say they would in his collection of eggs.

You talk about how being in awe too much can lead to inaction and defeat. What’s the evolutionary biological interpretation of this feeling of being faced with immense greatness? Is this feeling at all useful to humans?

I won’t say it can’t be, but I’m not in awe of awe. Situations create awe in us when we just can’t get it. It’s all too big for us. One of the psychological effects, and it can be measured, is that people feel small in the presence of awesome beauty. They literally draw themselves as smaller on the page. Their bodies shrink, and they feel a kind of humility. Humility is a fine emotion in the right place. It was felt, I would say, by Newton when he stood on the seashore and said that he felt like a child playing with pebbles on the beach, while the whole ocean of truth lay undiscovered before him. That’s an example of awe. But it’s not a feeling we want to submit to. The important thing is that we escape from it and say, “I’m not going to stop at this state of unknowing; I want to know the answers,” which, if we dig in the right place, we’ll begin to find.

Some of the most revered examples of feeling awe are associated with Buddhism, Zen Buddhism in particular. In the face of paradoxes, we’re encouraged to give up and to shrink and to dissolve our ego. Fine for meditating every now and again, but not as an attitude to life.

How much of our propensity for discovering rhyme do you think is conditioned? You give a very interesting example of the linguistic differences between French and Japanese, and English, and how these differences are actually mirrored in their designs for their gardens. So how much of one’s appreciation for beauty, what we might call their aesthetic expectations, is down to the culture and linguistic community that they’re a part of?

I suspect a lot, but it hasn’t really been studied. There’s been work on what’s called the linguistic relativity hypothesis, which has suggested that the words we use in our languages determine what distinctions we make in the world out there. Now, people haven’t missed the very simple fact that some languages have very many fewer syllables and many fewer words than English does. English is unique in just how rich it is in syllables and in words constructed from them. It means, rather surprisingly, that languages like Italian or Japanese have many more sound rhymes in them than English does. (It’s almost impossible not to rhyme in Japanese.) Therefore, one result is that the rhymes aren’t terribly interesting when they occur in Japanese or in Italian. Whereas in English, they have to be worked for. And that’s why I think poets have found the English language such a rich resource, because rhymes, when they’re brought to our attention by poets, suddenly stand out and make us think again about what’s going on here. I quote some literary theorists who have said that one of the functions of rhyme in poetry is precisely to make us see connections where they don’t exist or didn’t exist before. Two words rhyme. In the case of “cat” and “mat,” they don’t seem to have anything interesting in common, but again and again, in the hands of great poets, bringing words together (rhyming) makes them stand out as resembling each other, with the search for the meaning that lies behind that.

In the last chapter of your book, you talk about why, if we ever went to Mars, we wouldn’t find it beautiful. I thought this was a very interesting comparison to make. Is our world unique in that it has beauty? And as seekers of this beauty, doesn’t that put us humans in a very privileged position in the universe?

Yes, and I’m always arguing that humans are astonishingly privileged. I believe that life itself may be unique to our world, not necessarily, but life as it’s developed on Earth is certainly more complex, more interesting, more intricate, and certainly has developed levels of intelligence which are probably not found anywhere else in the known universe, and perhaps not in the universe as a whole. I’ve argued that human consciousness is an astonishing creation, which has depended on a whole chapter of accidents in the evolution of human beings, which almost certainly would never be repeated.

If we ran evolution again, we wouldn’t end up with human consciousness. And even if evolution ran on other planets, it most likely would not end up with human consciousness. So, yes, in the particular example of Mars, I say it is going to be different from the Earth simply because there is no life out there. And if we think about what makes for the rhymes of our world outside of the Earth, it’s very largely to do with animal and plant life, because they are the most extraordinary way of generating prodigious examples of rhyme. Plants and animals are by far the greatest source of rhyme in our world. But then when humans came along, we trumped that by then producing human artefacts, which rhyme at all sorts of levels, and producing language, which creates rhymes that have never existed before.

I think that if people are going to go to Mars and expect to be able to take photographs of new forms of natural beauty, they’re going to be disappointed; it’s going to be awfully dull. It comes down to this: there aren’t many things on Mars. Our Earth is loaded with things. There’s that nice rhyme by Stevenson, “The world is so full of a number of things, so I think we should all be so happy as kings.” You couldn’t say that about Mars, because there hasn’t been an evolutionary process at the level of geology, at the level of life, or at the level of intelligence, which has made the world so rich in discrete, nameable things. We have 80,000 words, 80,000 common nouns, for the kinds of things which exist around our world. We would be lucky if we could find 50 on Mars.

Nicholas, thank you very much for this conversation.

Nicholas Humphrey's latest book, Why Is the World So Beautiful? Our Minds in Search of Nature's Rhymes, is out on the 6th of October 2026 with MIT Press.
